Reasoning by 'cooling down' an LLM

Last edited 2026-11-22 · Draft

Summary.

  • We explore whether reinforcement learning can improve mathematical reasoning by sharpening an LLM's response distribution, without using ground-truth answers as training rewards.
  • On the Qwen models we tested, this improves accuracy with a few attempts, exceeding both low-temperature sampling and our MCMC baseline on MATH500. The recipe has not transferred reliably to OLMo and Llama model families: we observe empty answers, excessive shortening, or repetitive strings in different runs.
  • Likelihood diagnostics show substantial concentration, but the learned probabilities do not follow the intended power-law relation. What distribution the model actually learns remains an open question.

What is distribution sharpening?

A language model assigns probabilities to possible responses. Distribution sharpening increases the relative weight of responses the model already favors and suppresses less likely ones.

A principled way to define this is the power distribution. For a frozen base model p₀, a question x, and a response y, it is

The exponent α controls concentration, and Z normalizes the probabilities. At α=1, we recover the base distribution. For α>1, more likely responses gain relative weight. This says nothing by itself about correctness: sharpening can favor useful solutions, but it can also amplify confidently wrong behavior.

Here, “cooling down” refers to the distribution over complete responses. Lowering the temperature at each token generally produces a different distribution because it normalizes probabilities separately at every prefix.

How to obtain an LLM's power distribution?

There are two natural places to spend computation: during inference, by modifying the sampler, or during training, by changing the model's distribution.

Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). A sampler proposes changes to a response and accepts or rejects them using target and proposal probabilities. Reasoning with Sampling (Karan and Du, 2025) applies this idea through blockwise generation and response revisions, improving reasoning without changing model weights or using a correctness verifier. A finite run approximates power sampling and requires extra work for each new question.

Reinforcement Learning for Power Sampling (RLPS). We instead try to learn the power distribution directly. At a fixed response cap, minimizing reverse KL from a trainable policy π to the frozen base's power distribution is equivalent to minimizing

The omitted term, log Z, does not depend on the policy. The second term favors responses with high base likelihood. The first is negative policy entropy, which discourages putting all probability on one response. Together, their unrestricted optimum is the power distribution above. This connection is established in prior work, including Tomihari and Sato, 2026.

We optimize this objective with RLOO, an on-policy REINFORCE estimator with a leave-one-out baseline (Ahmadian et al., 2024). For each of B questions, we draw G responses from the current rollout policy. Each response receives the sequence-level reward

Subtracting the other responses' mean reward within the same question gives the advantage:

The surrogate loss used for the main results is

We treat the advantages as constants and take one optimizer step on each fresh batch. At the rollout policy, this estimates the gradient of J. Log probabilities sum over response tokens, including a sampled EOS, with prompt tokens excluded. Neither rewards nor baselines use answer correctness.

To stabilize training, we introduce sequence length warm-up: begin with a short response cap and increase it during training. This gradually expands the response space. After training, the policy uses ordinary autoregressive generation. In companion exploratory runs, discount ratio warm-up, which schedules the reward discount factor γ, has also helped stabilize training. It is a separate intervention from changing the power exponent α.

Experiments: Sharpening a base LLM's response on math problems

Our main experiment trains Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on MATH questions with α=2 and rank-eight LoRA. Each update samples four responses to each of 16 questions. The response cap starts at 32 tokens and increases by one token every two updates, ending at 512. We evaluate the checkpoint at the end of this schedule on all 500 MATH500 questions, using a 1,024-token cap and a prompt requesting step-by-step reasoning and a boxed answer.

We report pass@k: the probability that at least one of k independent responses is correct, averaged over questions.

Method Pass@1 Pass@2 Pass@4
Base, T=1 47.65% 64.03% 75.00%
Base, selected T=0.2 59.85% 69.20% 75.20%
MCMC, selected α=8 63.90% 70.17% 75.00%
GRPO with correctness rewards 59.60% 70.73% 79.00%
RLPS, T=1 67.30% 75.37% 80.60%

RLPS improves pass@1 by 19.65 percentage points over the base model, 7.45 points over the selected low temperature, and 3.40 points over the selected MCMC setting. Temperature and MCMC α were selected from our sweeps. These comparisons use equal numbers of returned answers, not equal compute. The MCMC row uses our finite-budget implementation, and GRPO uses a different training schedule as well as correctness labels.

Sequence length warm-up. In an auxiliary Qwen-0.5B/GSM8K experiment, we compare a fixed 256-token cap with sequence length warm-up from 64 to 256. Both runs use reward-to-go, 16 responses per question, and matching update and rollout counts.

Sequence length warm-up prevents a severe failure in this configuration. A decreasing training objective alone does not establish useful learning: concentrating on empty or trivial responses can also lower it.

Update (October 2026). After testing the method on more OLMo and Llama models, we found that sequence length warm-up and discount ratio warm-up do not always prevent collapse. On GSM8K, OLMo-1B still collapsed to immediate EOS. OLMo2-1B instead produced much shorter, nonempty answers, with greedy accuracy falling from 31.08% to 13.04%. We then tried normalizing the likelihood-based objective by response length. In exploratory OLMo and Llama runs, this led to a different failure mode: repetitive, low-entropy strings instead of useful reasoning.

Looking into the likelihood

If training sharpens the distribution, what changes in the answers it generates? We first ask whether those answers are more likely under the original model.

On a random subset of 50 MATH500 questions, we take 256 saved responses per question from each of Base, RLPS, and GRPO. We then score every response with the same frozen base model.

Mean base log likelihood per token rises from −0.284 on Base responses to −0.071 on RLPS responses. GRPO lies between them at −0.194. RLPS also follows prefixes at which the base has lower next-token entropy. The learned model samples from regions that the base considers more likely and is more confident about.

This successful run does not simply shorten its answers: separate probes at a fixed 1,024-token evaluation cap show mean response length increasing from about 604 to 681 tokens during training. Together, these diagnostics show a substantial change in the policy, but do not establish that it learned the particular power distribution we targeted.

Looking into the distribution

Comparing log likelihoods. An exact power distribution imposes a relationship between the two models' probabilities on each identical response:

The unknown normalizer depends on the question, but not on the response. Subtracting each scorer's mean log likelihood within a question removes it. With α=2, the centered policy score should then be twice the centered base score: every point should lie on a line of slope two.

We test this on the same 50-question subset, using all 256 Base responses and 256 RLPS responses per question. Centering is performed separately for each question and generating model.

The pooled fitted slopes are 0.983 on RLPS responses and 1.018 on Base responses, with standard deviations of 0.024 and 0.029 across question-specific slopes. Both are close to one rather than the target two. This diagnostic does not support exact exponent-two recovery. It probes sampled regions at an evaluation cap longer than the training cap, rather than measuring distance to the entire target distribution.

Comparing accuracy across sampling budgets. Does this redistribution expand the set of problems the model can solve? We independently sample 256 answers for every MATH500 question from Base, RLPS, and GRPO.

Both RLPS and GRPO outperform Base when only a few attempts are allowed. With enough attempts, Base catches up: pass@256 is 96.2% for Base, 96.0% for GRPO, and 95.6% for RLPS.

This pattern is consistent with the intuition behind sharpening: training makes already-accessible solutions more reliable, while some rare successful trajectories may lose probability. The curves alone do not prove that no new behaviors were learned. What they do show is a substantial gain in reliability with a few attempts, without a demonstrated expansion in coverage at 256 attempts.
